at skubbe.explanation: "At skubbe" means "to push". To tell someone to push a door open, the sign on the door says "Skub" (Push).

at skuffe.explanation: "At skuffe" means "to disappoint". To say you disappointed a person, put the person right after the verb, with no small word between: "Jeg skuffede dig" (I disappointed you). The noun "en skuffe" is a drawer: "Gaflerne ligger i skuffen" (The forks are in the drawer).

at skulle.explanation: "At skulle" means "to have to / should". To say you must do something, use "skal" before the verb: "Jeg skal arbejde" (I have to work). To say where you are going, use "skal" with a place: "Jeg skal i skole" (I am going to school).

at skumme.explanation: "At skumme" means "to foam / skim". When soap or milk makes foam, use it for foaming: "Sæben skummer" (The soap is foaming). When you read something quickly, use it for skimming: "skumme en artikel" (to skim an article).

at skyde.explanation: "At skyde" means "to shoot". To say a hunter shoots an animal, use it with the animal: "Jægeren skyder en hare" (The hunter shoots a hare). To say a player shoots in sports, use it with the ball: "Han skød bolden i mål" (He shot the ball into the goal).

at skylde.explanation: "At skylde" means "to owe". To say you owe someone money, use the person and the amount: "Jeg skylder dig hundrede kroner" (I owe you a hundred kroner). To say you blame someone, add "på" (on): "Han skylder på mig" (He blames me).

at skyldes.explanation: "At skyldes" means "to be due to". To name the reason for something, use it before the reason: "Problemet skyldes en fejl i systemet" (The problem is due to an error in the system). Do not mix it up with "at skylde" (to owe). To say you owe money, use "at skylde": "Jeg skylder dig hundrede kroner" (I owe you a hundred kroner).

at skylle.explanation: "At skylle" means "to rinse". To say you rinse something out, add "ud" (out): "Skyl munden ud" (Rinse your mouth out).

at skynde sig.explanation: "At skynde sig" means "to hurry". The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with who hurries: "Jeg skynder mig" (I hurry) and "Han skynder sig" (He hurries). To tell someone to hurry, say "Skynd dig!" (Hurry up!)

at skåle.explanation: "At skåle" means "to toast (with drinks)". To say who you toast, add "for" (for) before the person: "Vi skåler for dig" (We are toasting you).

at skåne.explanation: "At skåne" means "to spare". To say you go easy on a part of your body, use it with that part: "skåne sit knæ" (to go easy on your knee). To say you keep someone from something unpleasant, add "for" (from): "Jeg skåner dig for detaljerne" (I spare you the details).

at skælve.explanation: "At skælve" means "to tremble". To say you shake from cold, add "af" (from) and the cause: "Jeg skælver af kulde" (I am trembling from cold). The verb is part of "et jordskælv" (an earthquake), literally "an earth trembling".

at skændes.explanation: "At skændes" means "to argue". To say a group argues, use it with "vi" (we): "Vi skændes aldrig" (We never argue). To name the person you argue with, add "med" (with): "Jeg skændes med min bror" (I argue with my brother).

at skænke.explanation: "At skænke" means "to pour (a drink)". To offer to pour someone a drink, say: "Må jeg skænke en kop kaffe til dig?" (May I pour you a cup of coffee?) To say you give money as a gift, use "to donate" as the meaning: "skænke et beløb til en god sag" (to donate an amount to a good cause).

at skære.explanation: "At skære" means "to cut". To say you cut food with a knife, use it with the food: "Jeg skærer brødet i stykker" (I cut the bread into pieces). To cut paper with scissors, use "at klippe" (to cut with scissors) instead: "Jeg klipper papiret" (I cut the paper).

at skærpe.explanation: "At skærpe" means "to sharpen / tighten". It comes from the adjective "skarp" (sharp). To say you make rules stricter, use it with the rules: "skærpe reglerne" (to tighten the rules).

at sladre.explanation: "At sladre" means "to gossip / tell on". To say people talk about others, add "om" (about): "Naboerne sladrer om alt" (The neighbors gossip about everything). A child who tells on others is called "en sladrehank" (a tattletale).

at slanke sig.explanation: "At slanke sig" means "to diet". To say you diet, add "sig" (yourself), which changes with who diets: "Hun slanker sig" (She is dieting) and "Jeg slanker mig" (I am dieting).

at slappe af.explanation: "At slappe af" means "to relax". To say you relax in a place, add the place: "Jeg slapper af på sofaen" (I relax on the sofa). To tell someone to calm down, say "Slap af!" (Relax!)

at slentre.explanation: "At slentre" means "to stroll". To say you wander around with no goal, add "rundt" (around): "Vi slentrer rundt i byen" (We stroll around town).

at slette.explanation: "At slette" means "to delete". To tell someone to delete a message, use it with the message: "Slet beskeden" (Delete the message).

at slibe.explanation: "At slibe" means "to sharpen / sand". To say you make a knife sharp, use it with the knife: "Jeg sliber knivene" (I am sharpening the knives). To say you make wood smooth, use it with the furniture: "Jeg sliber bordet" (I am sanding the table).

at slide.explanation: "At slide" means "to wear out / toil". To say things wear out from use, use "slide op": "Skoene slides op, når man går meget i dem" (The shoes wear out when you walk a lot in them). To say someone works very hard, use the phrase "slide og slæbe" (to toil and drag).

at slikke.explanation: "At slikke" means "to lick". To say you lick an ice cream, use it with the ice cream: "at slikke en is" (to lick an ice cream). To say you lie in the sun, use "slikke sol" (literally, to lick sun).

at slippe.explanation: "At slippe" means "to let go / escape". To tell someone to let go of you, say "Slip mig!" (Let go of me!) To say someone got away, add "væk" (away): "Han slap væk" (He got away). To say you were spared from doing something, add "for" (from): "Jeg slap for at vaske op" (I got out of doing the dishes).

at slippe af med.explanation: "At slippe af med" means "to get rid of". It is built from "at slippe" (to escape) and "af med" (off with). To say you got rid of an illness, use it with the illness: "Hun slap af med sin forkølelse" (She got rid of her cold).

at sludre.explanation: "At sludre" means "to chat". To say you chat with someone, add "med" (with): "sludre med naboen" (to chat with the neighbor). The noun "sludder" means "nonsense": "Det er sludder!" (That is nonsense!)

at sluge.explanation: "At sluge" means "to swallow". To say you swallow a pill, use it with the pill: "Hun slugte tabletten uden vand" (She swallowed the pill without water). To say someone eats very fast, use it for "to gulp down": "Han slugte maden på to minutter" (He gulped the food down in two minutes).

at slukke.explanation: "At slukke" means "to turn off". To say you turn off a light, use it with the light: "slukke lyset" (turn off the light). To say you put out a fire, use it with the fire: "slukke en brand" (put out a fire). To turn off a TV, add "for" (for): "slukke for fjernsynet" (turn off the TV).

at slukke for.explanation: "At slukke for" means "to turn off". To say you turn off the TV, the radio or the heating, add "for" (for) after the verb: "Jeg slukker for radioen" (I turn off the radio). To say you put out a fire, use "at slukke" (to put out) with no "for": "slukke en brand" (to put out a fire).

at slutte.explanation: "At slutte" means "to end / finish". To say when something ends, use it with the time: "Skolen slutter klokken tre" (School ends at three). To say you stop doing something, add "med" (with) and "at" (to): "Jeg slutter med at ryge" (I am quitting smoking).

at slutte fred.explanation: "At slutte fred" means "to make peace". To name the person you make peace with, add "med" (with): "Jeg har sluttet fred med min bror" (I have made peace with my brother). To say you accept something that hurt you, use it for an inner struggle: "slutte fred med fortiden" (to make peace with the past).

at slå.explanation: "At slå" means "to hit / beat". To say you strike someone, use it with the person: "Slå ikke din bror!" (Do not hit your brother!) To say a team or player wins against another, use it for beating: "Vi slog dem tre-nul" (We beat them three to nothing). To say you cut a lawn, use it with the grass: "slå græsset" (mow the lawn).

at slå et smut forbi.explanation: "At slå et smut forbi" means "to drop by". To say the visit is short and casual, add "lige" (just): "Vi slår lige et smut forbi bageren" (We will just stop by the bakery).

at slå græs.explanation: "At slå græs" means "to mow the lawn". It is built from "slå" (hit) and "græs" (grass), so it is literally "to hit grass". To say you hit a ball, the same "slå" is used: "at slå en bold" (to hit a ball).

at slå igennem.explanation: "At slå igennem" means "to break through". To say someone becomes a star, use it for a career: "Hun slog igennem som sangerinde" (She became a star as a singer). To say the sun comes out from behind clouds, use it with the sun: "Solen slår igennem" (The sun breaks through).

at slå op.explanation: "At slå op" means "to look up". To say you look up a word, use it with the word: "Jeg slår ordet op" (I look up the word). To say you end a relationship, add "med" (with) and the partner: "Hun slog op med ham" (She broke up with him).

at slå sig ned.explanation: "At slå sig ned" means "to settle down". To say a family makes a new home somewhere, add the place: "Familien slog sig ned i Aarhus" (The family settled in Aarhus). To say you sit down for a while, use it with the place you sit: "Vi slog os ned på en bænk" (We took a seat on a bench).

at slå to fluer med et smæk.explanation: "At slå to fluer med et smæk" means "to kill two birds with one stone". Danish has two flies and one smack in this saying, not birds and a stone. It is built from "at slå" (to hit).

at slå ud.explanation: "At slå ud" means "to knock out". To say a team beats another team so it leaves the competition, use it with the losing team: "Danmark slog Tyskland ud" (Denmark knocked Germany out). To say trees come into leaf, use it with the trees: "Træerne slår ud i maj" (The trees come into leaf in May). To say a fuse cuts the power, use it with the fuse: "Sikringen slår ud" (The fuse trips).

at slæbe.explanation: "At slæbe" means "to drag". To say you carry or pull something heavy with effort, use it with the thing: "Han slæbte kufferten hen til bilen" (He dragged the suitcase to the car). To say you walk home with no energy, add "mig" (myself): "Jeg slæber mig hjem" (I drag myself home).

at smadre.explanation: "At smadre" means "to smash". To say a team beats an opponent by a lot, use it for a heavy defeat: "Holdet smadrede modstanderen" (The team beat the opponent badly). To say something is already smashed, use "smadret" (smashed): "Glasset er smadret" (The glass is smashed).

at smage.explanation: "At smage" means "to taste". To say you try food, use it with the food: "Jeg smager på suppen" (I taste the soup). To say how something tastes, use "Det smager godt" (It tastes good). To name the flavor, add "af" (of): "Det smager af citron" (It tastes like lemon).

at smelte.explanation: "At smelte" means "to melt". To say something melts by itself, use it with the thing: "Isen smelter i solen" (The ice melts in the sun). To say you melt something yourself, use it with the thing you melt: "Jeg smelter smør" (I melt butter).

at smide.explanation: "At smide" means "to throw (away)". To say you throw away trash, use it with the trash and the place: "Jeg smider papiret i skraldespanden" (I throw the paper in the trash can). To say you throw a ball to someone, use "at kaste" (to throw) instead: "Han kaster bolden til mig" (He throws the ball to me).

at smide ud.explanation: "At smide ud" means "to throw out". To say you throw out old food, use it with the food: "Jeg smider maden ud" (I throw the food out). To say someone is made to leave a place, use it with "af" (out of) and the place: "De smed ham ud af baren" (They threw him out of the bar).

at smile.explanation: "At smile" means "to smile". To say what or who you smile at, add "til" (to): "Smil til kameraet!" (Smile for the camera!)

at sminke sig.explanation: "At sminke sig" means "to put on makeup". To say who puts on makeup, change "sig" (oneself) with the person: "Hun sminker sig" (She puts on makeup) and "Du sminker dig" (You put on makeup).

at smitte.explanation: "At smitte" means "to infect". To say you pass an illness on to someone, use it with the person: "Jeg vil ikke smitte dig" (I do not want to infect you). To say a mood spreads, use it for laughter: "Hendes latter smitter" (Her laughter is catching).

at smugle.explanation: "At smugle" means "to smuggle". To say someone secretly brings a small thing into a place, use it with the thing and the place: "Han smuglede slik ind i biografen" (He smuggled candy into the movie theater).

at smuldre.explanation: "At smuldre" means "to crumble". To say food comes apart in small pieces, use it with the food: "Kagen smuldrer" (The cake crumbles). To say hopes fall apart, use it with the hopes: "Hans håb smuldrede" (His hopes crumbled).

at smutte.explanation: "At smutte" means "to slip away / pop out". To say you leave for a short moment, add "lige" (just): "Jeg smutter lige ud" (I will just pop out). To say something slips by accident, use it with the thing: "Kniven smuttede" (The knife slipped).

at smøre.explanation: "At smøre" means "to spread / butter". To say you put butter on bread, use it with the bread and "med" (with): "Jeg smører brødet med smør" (I spread butter on the bread). To say you make a packed lunch, use it with "en madpakke" (a packed lunch): "at smøre en madpakke" (to make a packed lunch).

at snakke.explanation: "At snakke" means "to talk / chat". To ask someone to talk with you, say: "Skal vi snakke sammen?" (Shall we talk together?)

at snakke om.explanation: "At snakke om" means "to talk about". To name the topic, put it after "om" (about): "Vi snakker om mad" (We are talking about food). To name the person you talk with, use "snakke med" (talk with): "Jeg snakker med min mor" (I talk with my mother).

at snakke om vejret.explanation: "At snakke om vejret" means "to make small talk", literally "to talk about the weather". To name another topic, replace "vejret" (the weather) with it: "snakke om fodbold" (to talk about football).

at sne.explanation: "At sne" means "to snow". To say it is snowing, use "det" (it): "Det sner" (It is snowing). The noun is spelled the same, "sne" (snow): "Der er sne" (There is snow).

at snige sig.explanation: "At snige sig" means "to sneak". To say which way you sneak, add a direction word: "at snige sig ind" (to sneak in) and "at snige sig ud" (to sneak out).

at snooze.explanation: "At snooze" means "to snooze". It is borrowed from the English word "snooze". To say you sleep late on purpose, use "at sove længe" (to sleep in): "I morgen sover jeg længe" (Tomorrow I will sleep in).

at snorke.explanation: "At snorke" means "to snore". To tell someone to stop, say: "Hold op med at snorke!" (Stop snoring!)

at snuble.explanation: "At snuble" means "to stumble". To name the thing you trip on, use "over" (over): "snuble over et kabel" (to trip over a cable). To say you hit a problem in a word, use it with a word: "snuble over et svært ord" (to stumble over a hard word).

at snuppe.explanation: "At snuppe" means "to snatch / grab". To say someone takes a thing quickly, use it with the thing: "Han snuppede min kuglepen" (He grabbed my pen). To suggest a quick small thing together, use it for "to grab": "Skal vi snuppe en kop kaffe?" (Shall we grab a cup of coffee?)

at snyde.explanation: "At snyde" means "to cheat". To say you cheat someone out of money, add "for" (of) and the amount: "Han snød mig for hundrede kroner" (He cheated me out of a hundred kroner).

at snøfte.explanation: "At snøfte" means "to sniffle". To say a child sniffles after crying, use it for the child: "Barnet snøftede længe bagefter" (The child sniffled for a long time afterward).

at sortere.explanation: "At sortere" means "to sort". To say you sort trash, use it with the trash: "Vi sorterer affald" (We sort the trash).

at sove.explanation: "At sove" means "to sleep". To say you sleep well, add "godt" (well): "Jeg sover godt" (I sleep well). To say you go to bed, use "at gå i seng" (to go to bed): "Jeg går i seng klokken ti" (I go to bed at ten).

at sove længe.explanation: "At sove længe" means "to sleep in". It is built from "at sove" (to sleep) and "længe" (a long time). To say you slept in, use it in the past: "Jeg sov længe i går" (I slept in yesterday).

at sove over sig.explanation: "At sove over sig" means "to oversleep", literally "to sleep over yourself". To say you overslept and were late, say: "Jeg sov over mig og kom for sent" (I overslept and was late). To sleep late on purpose, use "at sove længe" (to sleep in): "I morgen sover jeg længe" (Tomorrow I will sleep in).

at spadsere.explanation: "At spadsere" means "to stroll / walk". To say you go for a plain walk, use "at gå en tur" (to go for a walk): "Vi går en tur i skoven" (We go for a walk in the forest).

at spare.explanation: "At spare" means "to save (money)". To say you put money aside for a trip, use it with the money: "Vi sparer penge til en rejse" (We are saving money for a trip). To say something gives you more time, use it with "tid" (time): "Det sparer tid" (That saves time).

at spare op.explanation: "At spare op" means "to save up". To say what you save up for, add "til" (for): "Jeg sparer op til en cykel" (I am saving up for a bike). To say you save time, leave out "op" (up): "at spare tid" (to save time).

at spare på.explanation: "At spare på" means "to save on". To say you use less of something, use it with the thing: "Vi sparer på varmen" (We are saving on heat). To say you are careful with something, use it the same way: "Hun sparer på pengene" (She is careful with the money).

at sparke.explanation: "At sparke" means "to kick". To say you kick a ball, use it with the ball: "Han sparkede bolden over hegnet" (He kicked the ball over the fence). To say you give something one kick, add "til" (to): "Hun sparkede til døren" (She gave the door a kick).

at specialisere sig.explanation: "At specialisere sig" means "to specialize". To say the field, add "i" (in) after it: "at specialisere sig i hjertekirurgi" (to specialize in heart surgery).

at spejle.explanation: "At spejle" means "to mirror". It comes from the noun "et spejl" (a mirror). To say you look at your own image in a surface, add "sig" (yourself): "Hun spejler sig i vinduet" (She looks at herself in the window).

at spekulere.explanation: "At spekulere" means "to speculate / wonder". To name what you wonder about, add "på" (about): "Jeg spekulerer på det" (I wonder about that). To say you invest money in something, add "i" (in): "spekulere i aktier" (to speculate in shares).

at spilde.explanation: "At spilde" means "to waste / spill". To say liquid runs out by accident, use it with the liquid: "Jeg spildte vand på bordet" (I spilled water on the table). To say you waste something, use it with the thing: "Vi må ikke spilde mad" (We must not waste food).

at spilde tid.explanation: "At spilde tid" means "to waste time". To say what wastes your time, add "på" (on): "Jeg spilder tid på telefonen" (I waste time on the phone). The verb "at spilde" (to waste) also works without "tid" (time) to mean "to spill": "Jeg spildte kaffe" (I spilled coffee).

at spille.explanation: "At spille" means "to play". To say you play a game, a sport or an instrument, use it with that word: "Vi spiller fodbold" (We play soccer). To say an actor plays a part, use it with the part: "Hun spiller en prinsesse" (She plays a princess). To say children play for fun, use "at lege" (to play) instead: "Børnene leger i haven" (The children are playing in the garden).

at spille en rolle.explanation: "At spille en rolle" means "to play a role". To say someone acts a part on stage, use it with the place: "Hun spiller en rolle i skolens teater" (She plays a role in the school theater). To say something does not matter, use it with "ikke nogen" (not any): "Prisen spiller ikke nogen rolle" (The price does not matter).

at spille fodbold.explanation: "At spille fodbold" means "to play soccer". The word "fodbold" is built from "fod" (foot) and "bold" (ball). The verb "at spille" (to play) works for other sports too: "spille håndbold" (to play handball).

at spise.explanation: "At spise" means "to eat". To say you eat at a restaurant, add "ude" (out): "Vi spiser ude i aften" (We are eating out tonight). To say you drink, use "at drikke" (to drink) instead: "Jeg drikker vand" (I drink water).

at sponsorere.explanation: "At sponsorere" means "to sponsor". To say a company pays for an event, use it with the event: "Firmaet sponsorerer kampen" (The company sponsors the match). The person or company that does it is "en sponsor" (a sponsor).

at spore.explanation: "At spore" means "to track / trace". It is built on "et spor" (a trail or footprint). To say you trace where a call came from, use it with the call: "spore et opkald" (to trace a call).

at sprede.explanation: "At sprede" means "to spread". To say something spreads by itself, add "sig" (itself): "Rygtet spreder sig" (The rumor spreads). To say someone spreads something, leave out "sig": "Han spreder rygtet" (He spreads the rumor).

at springe.explanation: "At springe" means "to jump". To say you skip a page, add "over" (over): "Jeg springer en side over" (I skip a page).

at springe over.explanation: "At springe over" means "to skip". To say you leave out a meal, use it with the meal: "Jeg springer frokosten over" (I skip lunch). To say you jump across something, use it with the thing: "Hunden sprang over hegnet" (The dog jumped over the fence).

at sprænge.explanation: "At sprænge" means "to blow up". To say explosives destroy something, use it with the thing: "at sprænge en bro" (to blow up a bridge). To say you go over a limit, use it with the limit: "at sprænge budgettet" (to blow the budget).

at sprøjte.explanation: "At sprøjte" means "to spray". The noun "en sprøjte" (a syringe) is spelled the same way: "Lægen giver mig en sprøjte" (The doctor gives me an injection).

at spytte.explanation: "At spytte" means "to spit". To say where you spit, add "på" (on): "spytte på gulvet" (spit on the floor). To say a dragon breathes out fire, use it with the fire: "Dragen spytter ild" (The dragon spits fire).

at spænde.explanation: "At spænde" means "to tighten / fasten". To tell someone to pull a strap tight, say: "Spænd remmen" (Tighten the strap). To say you tense your body, use it with the muscles: "Jeg spænder musklerne" (I tense my muscles).

at spøge.explanation: "At spøge" means "to joke". To say you are not serious, add "kun" (only): "Jeg spøger kun" (I am only joking). To say a ghost is in a place, use "det" (it) and the place: "Det spøger i huset" (The house is haunted).

at spørge.explanation: "At spørge" means "to ask". To ask a person about something, add "om" (about): "Jeg spørger ham om vejen" (I ask him about the way). To ask for something you want, use "at bede om" (to ask for) instead: "Jeg beder om en kop kaffe" (I ask for a cup of coffee).

at spørge om.explanation: "At spørge om" means "to ask about". To ask about a thing, put it after "om" (about): "spørge om prisen" (ask about the price). To ask for something you need, use it the same way: "spørge om hjælp" (ask for help).

at spørge om vej.explanation: "At spørge om vej" means "to ask for directions", literally "to ask about way". To stop a stranger and ask, say: "Undskyld, må jeg spørge om vej?" (Excuse me, may I ask for directions?)

at stabilisere.explanation: "At stabilisere" means "to stabilize". To say something steadies by itself, add "sig" (itself): "Priserne stabiliserer sig" (The prices stabilize).

at stadfæste.explanation: "At stadfæste" means "to confirm / uphold". To say a court keeps a decision, use it with the decision: "Retten stadfæstede dommen" (The court upheld the verdict).

at stamme.explanation: "At stamme" means "to stutter / come from". To say someone stutters, use it alone: "Han stammer, når han er nervøs" (He stutters when he is nervous). To say where something comes from, add "fra" (from): "Min familie stammer fra Jylland" (My family comes from Jutland).

at standse.explanation: "At standse" means "to stop". To say a vehicle comes to a halt, use it with the vehicle: "Bilen standsede foran huset" (The car stopped in front of the house). To say you quit a habit, use "at holde op" (to quit) instead: "Jeg holder op med at ryge" (I am quitting smoking).

at starte.explanation: "At starte" means "to start". To say an event begins, use it with the time: "Vi starter i morgen" (We start tomorrow). To say a machine will not run, use it with the machine: "Bilen starter ikke" (The car will not start). To say a lesson begins, "at begynde" (to begin) works too: "Timen begynder klokken ni" (The lesson begins at nine).
